title: Matrix multiplication, one cell at a time
intro: Learn how input features and weights combine, then apply the same operation to a batch.

steps.title: Check the dimensions
steps.body: A has two rows and three columns: [[1, 2, 0], [−1, 1, 3]]. B has three rows and two columns: [[2, 0], [1, 4], [3, −1]]. The inner dimensions match, so C has two rows and two columns.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.body: C = [[4, 8], [8, 1]]. Each output cell combines one row of A and one column of B. A neural-network layer repeats this pattern with learned weights.

steps.title: Add bias and batch inputs
steps.body: With examples stored as columns, a dense layer can use Y = WX + b, broadcasting the output-sized bias across examples. Some libraries store examples as rows and transpose the weights; the underlying dot products are the same.

limits: The numbers are illustrative. Matrix storage conventions must be stated before comparing formulas.

title: Backpropagation: calculate a complete update
intro: Follow a prediction, squared error and gradient update through one neuron.

steps.title: Make a prediction
steps.body: Let x = 2, w = 3 and b = 1. The target is y = 5. The prediction is ŷ = wx + b = 7.

steps.title: Measure the error
steps.body: The error is 7 − 5 = 2 and the squared loss is 4. The derivative with respect to the prediction is 2(ŷ − y) = 4.

steps.title: Apply the chain rule
steps.body: Since ∂ŷ/∂w = x = 2, the weight gradient is 4×2 = 8. Since ∂ŷ/∂b = 1, the bias gradient is 4.

steps.title: Update the parameters
steps.body: With learning rate η = 0.1, w′ = 3 − 0.1×8 = 2.2 and b′ = 1 − 0.1×4 = 0.6. The new prediction is 5 and the loss is zero for this one example.

steps.title: Extend to hidden layers
steps.body: For a hidden layer, multiply by the downstream weights and the activation derivative. ReLU contributes a derivative of one on positive inputs and zero on negative inputs. Its behavior at zero depends on the chosen convention.

limits: A perfect fit to one example says nothing about generalization. For mean squared error over n examples, averaging introduces a factor of 1/n.

title: Softmax and next-token sampling
intro: Turn scores into probabilities and select a token from a cumulative distribution.

steps.title: Choose simple scores
steps.body: Use scores [0, ln 2, ln 3]. Their exponentials are [1, 2, 3], whose sum is 6.

steps.title: Normalize
steps.body: The probabilities are [1/6, 2/6, 3/6]. They sum to one. In implementations, subtracting the largest score before exponentiation improves numerical stability without changing the probabilities.

steps.title: Build cumulative intervals
steps.body: For tokens A, B and C, the cumulative intervals are [0, 1/6), [1/6, 1/2) and [1/2, 1). A uniform draw of 0.65 selects C.

steps.title: Generate another token
steps.body: Append the selected token and recompute the model’s distribution for the next position. A new prediction depends on the updated context.

steps.title: Understand temperature
steps.body: Dividing scores by a positive temperature before softmax changes how concentrated the distribution is. Lower temperatures favor higher-scoring tokens more strongly; they do not guarantee correctness.

limits: Token probabilities describe the model’s next-token distribution, not the truth of a sentence.

title: Self-attention with two tokens
intro: Calculate attention weights and the weighted combination of values.

steps.title: State the convention
steps.body: Represent tokens as rows. Let Q = K = [[1, 0], [0, 1]], and V = [[2, 0], [0, 4]]. There are two key dimensions, so dₖ = 2.

steps.title: Compare queries and keys
steps.body: QKᵀ is the identity matrix. Scaling by √2 gives [[0.7071, 0], [0, 0.7071]].

steps.title: Normalize each query row
steps.body: Applying softmax across each row gives approximately [[0.6698, 0.3302], [0.3302, 0.6698]]. Each row sums to one.

steps.title: Combine the values
steps.body: The first output is 0.6698[2,0] + 0.3302[0,4] ≈ [1.3396,1.3208]. The second is approximately [0.6604,2.6792].

steps.title: Add the real-world pieces
steps.body: A transformer learns the query, key and value projections and commonly uses multiple heads, residual paths, normalization and a feed-forward block. Causal masks prevent access to future positions when required.

limits: The source exercise approximated exponentials and scaling for hand calculation. This example uses the actual softmax operation; it is still a tiny illustration.

title: Batch normalization and dropout by example
intro: Compare two operations that affect training in very different ways.

steps.title: Normalize a feature
steps.body: For one feature across a batch [1, 3], the mean is 2 and the population variance is 1. Ignoring a very small ε for this hand calculation gives normalized values [−1, 1].

steps.title: Learn scale and shift
steps.body: With learned scale γ = 2 and offset β = 0.5, the outputs become [−1.5, 2.5]. Batch normalization tracks statistics and uses configured evaluation behavior; layer normalization normalizes over different dimensions.

steps.title: Apply a dropout mask
steps.body: For activations [2, 4] and dropout probability p = 0.5, suppose the first activation is kept and the second is dropped. Inverted dropout returns [4, 0].

steps.title: Explain the scaling
steps.body: The kept value is divided by 1−p. Across random masks this preserves the expected activation. At evaluation time, standard inverted dropout acts as the identity.

steps.title: Keep their roles distinct
steps.body: Normalization rescales features using statistics and learned parameters. Dropout randomly removes activations during training. Neither guarantees better performance in every setting.

limits: Training and evaluation behavior must be distinguished. Libraries may use different estimators for running variance.

title: Recurrent and state-space models: follow the state
intro: See how a sequence changes a hidden state, including the source’s small state-space calculation.

steps.title: Start from zero
steps.body: Use h₀ = [0,0], A = [[1,0],[0,−1]], B = [−1,2] and C = [−2,−3]. The first input is x₁ = 3.

steps.title: Process a second input
steps.body: Keeping these toy parameters fixed, let x₂ = 1. Then Ah₁ = [−3,−6], so h₂ = [−4,−4] and y₂ = 8 + 12 = 20.

steps.title: Compare with an RNN
steps.body: A simple RNN commonly applies a nonlinearity to its state update. This linear state-space example does not. More advanced selective state-space systems can make components input-dependent and use discretization and additional structure.

limits: This recurrence explains state updates; it is not a full implementation of Mamba or its selective mechanism.

title: Mixture of experts: routing and capacity
intro: Follow tokens through a router and understand what sparse computation means.

steps.title: Read the scores
steps.body: Suppose token A receives expert scores [0.1, 0.8, 0.1] and token B receives [0.7, 0.2, 0.1]. A top-one router selects expert two for A and expert one for B.

steps.title: Use the chosen experts
steps.body: Only the selected expert processes each token in this simplified example. The experts have distinct parameters; the same token representation need not produce the same output in every expert.

steps.title: Respect capacity
steps.body: If an expert can accept two tokens in a batch and three route to it, the system needs a defined overflow policy. Dropping, rerouting and residual handling are design choices, not universal behavior.

steps.title: Train the routing system
steps.body: Practical systems can use routing weights and auxiliary objectives to balance utilization. Total parameter count and parameters activated per token are different quantities.

limits: The source omitted scaling and simplified overflow. No exact proprietary model behavior is inferred from that sketch.

title: Residual connections and graph messages
intro: Calculate a skip connection and aggregate neighboring node features.

steps.title: Add the skip path
steps.body: Let x = [2,−1] and F(x) = [1,3]. A residual addition gives [3,2]. Shapes must match, or a projection is needed.

steps.title: Separate addition from concatenation
steps.body: Concatenating the two vectors gives [2,−1,1,3], which has four components. It is a different operation; a later matrix can implement a sum, but concatenation alone is not residual addition.

steps.title: Aggregate graph neighbors
steps.body: For a node with feature [1,2] and a neighbor with feature [3,1], a simple sum including the node itself is [4,3]. Repeating message passing lets information travel across more edges.

steps.title: Understand the actual graph layer
steps.body: Graph convolution variants can normalize adjacency, transform features and apply nonlinearities. A raw sum illustrates aggregation but does not specify the normalization or learned operation of a particular GCN.

limits: The source diagram’s matrix stacking is a visualization device. The guide distinguishes it from the residual addition itself.

title: Autoencoders, GANs and diffusion: training objectives
intro: Compare reconstruction, adversarial learning and noise prediction with small examples.

steps.title: Reconstruct an input
steps.body: An autoencoder maps x = [2,0] through an encoder and decoder. If the reconstruction is [1.5,0.5], mean squared error is (0.25+0.25)/2 = 0.25. The gradient with respect to the reconstruction is [−0.5,0.5].

steps.title: Train an adversary
steps.body: A discriminator learns to distinguish real and generated examples; a generator learns to produce examples the discriminator accepts. With sigmoid output and binary cross-entropy, the derivative with respect to the logit is prediction minus target, subject to the chosen reduction.

steps.title: Predict noise
steps.body: A diffusion training example adds noise according to a schedule. If sampled noise is [1,−1] and predicted noise is [0.8,−0.6], the two-component mean squared error is (0.04+0.16)/2 = 0.10.

steps.title: Sample using the specified process
steps.body: Generation uses the model and a sampling rule to iteratively transform noise. Simply subtracting a predicted vector once is not a general diffusion sampler.

steps.title: Distinguish architectures
steps.body: A diffusion transformer can process latent patches and conditioning. An illustrative patch diagram cannot establish a commercial video model’s exact encoder, schedule or parameter values.

limits: The source simplified noise schedules and generation. The corrected example states the objective without claiming those simplifications are a production algorithm.

title: Vector retrieval: calculate similarity and rank results
intro: Work through pooling, cosine similarity and an exact search before considering approximate indexes.

steps.title: Pool token features
steps.body: For token vectors [1,0] and [1,2], mean pooling produces [1,1]. Pooling must match the embedding model’s design; mean pooling is not universally appropriate.

steps.title: Score two candidates
steps.body: For query q = [1,0], candidate A = [2,0] has dot product 2 and cosine similarity 1. Candidate B = [1,1] has dot product 1 and cosine similarity 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071.

steps.title: Choose the metric deliberately
steps.body: Dot product depends on vector magnitude. Cosine similarity removes that effect. A model’s training and index configuration determine the appropriate metric.

steps.title: Scale search
steps.body: An exact scan scores every vector. Approximate nearest-neighbor indexes trade some recall for speed or memory efficiency; evaluate retrieval quality and filtering together.

steps.title: Preserve permissions
steps.body: Retain source identifiers and access metadata. Similarity does not establish whether a passage is true or whether a user may access it.

limits: Random projection, dimensionality reduction and vector indexing are distinct operations; an embedding database does not necessarily require the projection step shown in the source.

title: Learning from human preferences: a reward example
intro: Understand pairwise reward learning and what it does—and does not—establish.

steps.title: Collect a comparison
steps.body: A reviewer compares two responses to the same prompt under stated criteria. Preferences depend on instructions, reviewer judgment and the examples collected.

steps.title: Calculate the reward gap
steps.body: Use source reward values 5 for the preferred response and 3 for the other. The difference is 2. Sigmoid(2) ≈ 0.8808, rather than exactly 0.9.

steps.title: Measure pairwise loss
steps.body: For the preferred outcome, the negative log-likelihood is −ln(0.8808) ≈ 0.1269. The derivative with respect to the gap is sigmoid(2)−1 ≈ −0.1192.

steps.title: Update and use the reward model
steps.body: Backpropagation can improve preference prediction. A later policy optimization step may use reward feedback with additional constraints; training a reward model alone does not complete RLHF.

steps.title: Watch for reward mismatch
steps.body: A system can optimize a reward while missing the human goal. Preference agreement is not proof of factual accuracy, fairness or safety.

limits: The original preference example’s social judgment is not treated as universally correct. The mathematical example concerns a declared preferred pair.
